chapter: Los Angeles, Central Avenue and the Apex
title: Bing Crosby: Prohibition nightlife and a 1977 Concord concert
summary: After-hours crowds from the Coconut Grove came to the Apex; Royal recalls Bing Crosby's early hits and his poised handling of a sound failure at Concord weeks before his death.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: Prohibition time and that was one of the few places where you could go and find a first-class nightclub that went on until four and five o'clock in the morning. After everything was over in Hollywood at the Coconut Grove, they started heading toward the Apex. That's where it was. That was just a little bit before Bing Crosby went to work in the Coconut Grove with Gus Arnheim (PHONETIC). I was working at the Sebastian's Hide Cotton Club with Les Haight (PHONETIC) at the time that Bing Crosby was doing his -- making his big hits like "Just One More Chance," "Wrap Your Troubles in Dreams," "Stardust," and things like that, when he actually was trying to sing his way back home to Dixie, his wife, because he was such a drunk in those days, God bless his soul. He just passed. But he was trying to sing his way back into the good feelings of his home with his wife, Dixie, and he was really pouring it out and that helped make a lot of his things very popular, from the way that he sang them with the true sincerity that he was trying to put down at that time.

As a matter of fact, I was fortunate enough to appear with one of Bing's last concerts, at the Concord Jazz up in Concord, California, two months ago, right before he went on his European tour. So, seeing that he just passed last week, I think it was a very fortunate thing to be able to be a part of him again in his waning days. He was a pretty good man, as singers go.
Was he in good voice at the concert?

Excellent. The thing happened up there that was really out of sight, as the jargon of the word game goes today. He came on to do his first number and after he did his first number, the complete sound system went out. He was appearing before a sell-out crowd in this new Concord Jazz Festival Arena, which had about 7,000 people in it, and he was so cool and professional. When it went out, he never left the stage. He just stood up on stage, waved to the people, talked to a few people in the audience, and had Joey Bushkin, who was his piano player, accompanist, along with his four-piece group, to entertain the people until the mike system was fixed and Joey Bushkin went on and did his thing. Bing never left the stage, stayed out there with him. The people took it all just beautifully. Not a soul left. When the sound system came back on, he went right on, did his number, and received standing ovations all night and never lost his cool.

When a lot of the lesser professionals would have blown their wig and made a scene, this big pro of them all just stood there and just took it like it was and waited until everything was put into working order and went on the stage and broke it up. This is beautiful. That's a pro. That's great.
